doc.title: Ruth Lion interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Francis Wolff's photography
summary: Frank preferred black and white, expressing the artists' soul, and later shot some colour.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Now as we look back on it, it is such a wonderful legacy that the fact that it eventually was sold, I don’t think it matters now. I think, look at what the product was. Priceless. And one thing we didn’t even bring up, really yet, is the marvelous photography that is such a part of that. And I’m curious if Frank ever experimented with color, with his photography? Did he ever shoot in color? Because most of it’s all black and white, his photos, and they work so well.

He thought, I believe, that black and white was more artistic. And he did experiment toward the last, and then of course when Blue Note was sold to United Artists and he did more in color. And I have those also. But I prefer the black and white because I think they express the soul of the artist. You know, he was looking for that. He would stand with his light and looking over, he would stand forever, to get that shot he wanted to get. And when you see those pictures you know, they’re really art.

Yes, absolutely. It’s a whole other contribution of Blue Note, that those photographs stand on their own. To have that with the music, hey, there is heaven. That’s great. We had looked at some of the gold records and so forth, and really great mementos that you have from those days. Tell me about the tribute in Japan.
